newsitem.title: USA: Teens believe tobacco ads aimed at them - survey.
newsitem.headline: Teens believe tobacco ads aimed at them - survey.

text.p: Most U.S. teenagers believe that tobacco companies aim their advertising campaigns at them and support laws to curb smoking by children, according to a survey released Tuesday by an anti-smoking group.

The National Center for Tobacco Free Kids, a group backed by health organizations, sponsored a nationwide survey of 513 teen-agers that found three out of four believe cigarette companies are advertising to them.

The finding counters tobacco company claims that such popular ad campaigns as Joe Camel and the Marlboro Man are not targeting the teen-age market. A Federal Trade Commission study released in 1994 sided with the tobacco industry.

Nine out of 10 of those surveyed believe stores should keep cigarettes out of their reach and demand proof they are over 18 years old before selling tobacco products, and that ads should not be allowed close to schools or playgrounds.

Seventy-three percent favored a ban on advertisements in magazines they read. Sixty-six percent supported a ban on sponsoring or advertising at concerts or sporting events and 63 percent supported outlawing tobacco ads on T-shirts, hats, backpacks or other items used by teen-agers.

Dr. Richard Heyman, chairman of the American Academy of Pediatrics panel on substance abuse, told a news conference that 90 percent of all those who ever smoke start before they turn 19, most at around the age of 12.

"The image of smokers has been cleverly crafted by the tobacco industry to lure kids into smoking by turning cigarettes into symbols," Heyman said, adding the industry spent some $6 billion a year on advertising and promotion.
An estimated 35 percent of American high school students smoke, according the Centers for Disease Control surveys.

Tom Lauria, a spokesman for the main industry trade group, the Tobacco Institute, said the survey showed only "that with very heavy prompting, kids told them what they wanted to hear." He cited the way questions were posed in the survey, which has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percent.
"The FTC concluded in 1994 that cigarette advertising is not aimed at prompting kids to smoke," Lauria said.
The Food and Drug Administration has proposed measures to curb teen-age smoking, including restrictions on vending machines, advertising and sponsoring concerts and other events.
